{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
[[File:Plot of the Jacobi polynomial function P n^(a,b) with n=10 and a=2 and b=2 in the complex plane from -2-2i to 2+2i with colors created with Mathematica 13.1 function ComplexPlot3D.svg|alt=Plot of the Jacobi polynomial function P n^(a,b) with n=10 and a=2 and b=2 in the complex plane from -2-2i to 2+2i with colors created with Mathematica 13.1 function ComplexPlot3D|thumb|Plot of the Jacobi polynomial function <math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}</math> with <math>n=10</math> and <math>\alpha=2</math> and <math>\beta=2</math> in the complex plane from <math>-2-2i</math> to <math>2+2i</math> with colors created with Mathematica 13.1 function ComplexPlot3D]]
In [[mathematics]], '''Jacobi polynomials''' (occasionally called '''hypergeometric polynomials''') <math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)</math>
are a class of [[Classical orthogonal polynomials|classical]] [[orthogonal polynomials]]. They are orthogonal with respect to the weight
<math>(1-x)^\alpha(1+x)^\beta</math> on the interval <math>[-1,1]</math>. The [[Gegenbauer polynomials]], and thus also the [[Legendre polynomials|Legendre]], [[Zernike polynomials|Zernike]] and [[Chebyshev polynomials]], are special cases of the Jacobi polynomials.<ref name="sz">{{Harvard citation|Szegő|1975|loc=4. Jacobi polynomials}}</ref>

The Jacobi polynomials were introduced by [[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi]].

==Definitions==

===Via the hypergeometric function===
The Jacobi polynomials are defined via the [[hypergeometric function]] as follows:<ref>{{Abramowitz_Stegun_ref|22|561}}</ref><ref name="sz" />{{Pg|location=IV.1}}

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z)=\frac{(\alpha+1)_n}{n!}\,{}_2F_1\left(-n,1+\alpha+\beta+n;\alpha+1;\tfrac{1}{2}(1-z)\right),</math>

where <math>(\alpha+1)_n</math> is [[Pochhammer symbol|Pochhammer's symbol]] (for the rising factorial). In this case, the series for the hypergeometric function is finite, therefore one obtains the following equivalent expression:

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} (z) = \frac{\Gamma (\alpha+n+1)}{n!\,\Gamma (\alpha+\beta+n+1)} \sum_{m=0}^n {n\choose m} \frac{\Gamma (\alpha + \beta + n + m + 1)}{\Gamma (\alpha + m + 1)} \left(\frac{z-1}{2}\right)^m.</math>

===Rodrigues' formula===
An equivalent definition is given by [[Rodrigues' formula]]:<ref name=sz/>{{Pg|location=IV.3}}<ref>{{SpringerEOM|title=Jacobi polynomials|author=P.K. Suetin}}</ref>

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z) = \frac{(-1)^n}{2^n n!} (1-z)^{-\alpha} (1+z)^{-\beta} \frac{d^n}{dz^n} \left\{ (1-z)^\alpha (1+z)^\beta \left (1 - z^2 \right )^n \right\}.</math>

If <math> \alpha = \beta = 0 </math>, then it reduces to the [[Legendre polynomials]]: 
:<math> P_{n}(z) = \frac{1 }{2^n  n! } \frac{d^n }{ d z^n }  ( z^2 - 1 )^n  \; .  </math>

=== Differential equation ===
The Jacobi polynomials <math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}</math> is, up to scaling, the unique polynomial solution of the [[Sturm–Liouville theory|Sturm–Liouville problem]]<ref name="sz" />{{Pg|location=IV.2}}
:<math> \left (1-x^2 \right )y'' + ( \beta-\alpha - (\alpha + \beta + 2)x )y' = \lambda y</math>
where <math> \lambda = -n(n+\alpha+\beta+1)</math>. The other solution involves the logarithm function. [[Bochner's theorem (orthogonal polynomials)|Bochner's theorem]] states that the Jacobi polynomials are uniquely characterized as polynomial solutions to Sturm–Liouville problems with polynomial coefficients.

=== Alternate expression for real argument ===
For real <math>x</math> the Jacobi polynomial can alternatively be written as

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)= \sum_{s=0}^n {n+\alpha\choose n-s}{n+\beta \choose s} \left(\frac{x-1}{2}\right)^{s} \left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)^{n-s}</math>

and for integer <math>n</math>

:<math>{z \choose n} = \begin{cases} \frac{\Gamma(z+1)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(z-n+1)} & n \geq 0 \\ 0 & n < 0 \end{cases}</math>

where <math>\Gamma(z)</math> is the [[gamma function]].

In the special case that the four quantities <math>n</math>, <math>n+\alpha</math>, <math>n+\beta</math>, <math>n+\alpha+\beta</math>
are nonnegative integers, the Jacobi polynomial can be written as

{{NumBlk|:|<math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)=(n+\alpha)! (n+\beta)! \sum_{s=0}^n \frac{1}{s! (n+\alpha-s)!(\beta+s)!(n-s)!} \left(\frac{x-1}{2}\right)^{n-s} \left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)^{s}.</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

The sum extends over all integer values of <math>s</math> for which the arguments of the factorials are nonnegative.

===Special cases===

:<math>P_0^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z)= 1,</math>
:<math>P_1^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z)= (\alpha+1) + (\alpha+\beta+2)\frac{z-1}{2},</math>

:<math>P_2^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z)= \frac{(\alpha+1)(\alpha+2)}{2}
+ (\alpha+2)(\alpha+\beta+3)\frac{z-1}{2}

+ \frac{(\alpha+\beta+3)(\alpha+\beta+4)}{2}\left(\frac{z-1}{2}\right)^2.</math>
<math display="block">P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(z)=\frac{\Gamma(1 + 2 n+\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(1 + n)\Gamma(1 + n+\alpha+\beta)}\left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^n+\text { lower-degree terms }</math>Thus, the leading coefficient is <math>\frac{\Gamma(1 + 2 n+\alpha+\beta)}{2^nn! \Gamma(1 + n+\alpha+\beta)}</math>.

==Basic properties==

===Orthogonality===
The Jacobi polynomials satisfy the orthogonality condition

:<math>\int_{-1}^1 (1-x)^{\alpha} (1+x)^{\beta} P_m^{(\alpha,\beta)} (x)P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} (x)\,dx =\frac{2^{\alpha+\beta+1}}{2n+\alpha+\beta+1} \frac{\Gamma(n+\alpha+1)\Gamma(n+\beta+1)}{\Gamma(n+\alpha+\beta+1)n!} \delta_{nm}, \qquad \alpha,\ \beta > -1.</math>

As defined, they do not have unit norm with respect to the weight. This can be corrected by dividing by the square root of the right hand side of the equation above, when <math>n=m</math>.

Although it does not yield an [[orthonormal basis]], an alternative normalization is sometimes preferred due to its simplicity:

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)} (1) = {n+\alpha\choose n}.</math>

===Symmetry relation===
The polynomials have the symmetry relation

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)} (-z) = (-1)^n P_n^{(\beta, \alpha)} (z);</math>

thus the other terminal value is

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)} (-1) = (-1)^n { n+\beta\choose n}.</math>

===Derivatives===
The <math>k</math>th derivative of the explicit expression leads to

:<math>\frac{d^k}{dz^k} P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} (z) = \frac{\Gamma (\alpha+\beta+n+1+k)}{2^k \Gamma (\alpha+\beta+n+1)} P_{n-k}^{(\alpha+k, \beta+k)} (z).</math>

===Recurrence relations===
The 3-term [[Orthogonal polynomials#Recurrence relation|recurrence relation]] for the Jacobi polynomials of fixed <math>\alpha</math>, <math>\beta</math> is:<ref name=sz/>{{Pg|location=IV.5}}

:<math>
\begin{align}
&2n (n + \alpha + \beta) (2n + \alpha + \beta - 2) P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z) \\
&\qquad= (2n+\alpha + \beta-1) \Big\{ (2n+\alpha + \beta)(2n+\alpha+\beta-2) z +  \alpha^2 - \beta^2 \Big\} P_{n-1}^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z) - 2 (n+\alpha - 1) (n + \beta-1) (2n+\alpha + \beta) P_{n-2}^{(\alpha, \beta)}(z),
\end{align}
</math>

for <math>n=2,3,\ldots</math>.
Writing for brevity <math>a:=n + \alpha </math>, <math>b:=n + \beta</math> and  <math>c:=a+b=2n + \alpha+ \beta</math>, this becomes in terms of <math>a,b,c </math>
:<math> 2n (c-n)(c-2) P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z) =(c-1) \Big\{ c(c-2) z + (a-b)(c-2n) \Big\} P_{n-1}^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z)-2 (a-1)(b-1) c\; P_{n-2}^{(\alpha, \beta)}(z). </math>
  
Since the Jacobi polynomials can be described in terms of the hypergeometric function, recurrences of the hypergeometric function give equivalent recurrences of the Jacobi polynomials. In particular, Gauss' [[Hypergeometric function#Gauss's contiguous relations|contiguous relations]] correspond to the identities<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/pec27/urdf | first1=P. E. | last1=Creasey | title = A Unitary BRDF for Surfaces with Gaussian Deviations | website=[[GitHub]] }}</ref>{{Pg|location=Appx.B}}

:<math>
\begin{align}
(z-1) \frac{d}{dz} P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z) 
& = \frac{1}{2} (z-1)(1+\alpha+\beta+n)P_{n-1}^{(\alpha+1,\beta+1)} \\
& = n P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} - (\alpha+n) P_{n-1}^{(\alpha,\beta+1)} \\
& =(1+\alpha+\beta+n) \left( P_n^{(\alpha,\beta+1)} - P_{n}^{(\alpha,\beta)} \right) \\
& =(\alpha+n) P_n^{(\alpha-1,\beta+1)} - \alpha P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} \\
& =\frac{2(n+1) P_{n+1}^{(\alpha,\beta-1)} - \left(z(1+\alpha+\beta+n)+\alpha+1+n-\beta \right) P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}}{1+z} \\
& =\frac{(2\beta+n+nz) P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} - 2(\beta+n) P_n^{(\alpha,\beta-1)}}{1+z} \\
& =\frac{1-z}{1+z} \left( \beta P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)} - (\beta+n) P_{n}^{(\alpha+1,\beta-1)} \right) \, .
\end{align}
</math>

===Generating function===
The [[generating function]] of the Jacobi polynomials is given by

:<math> \sum_{n=0}^\infty P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(z) t^n = 2^{\alpha + \beta} R^{-1} (1 - t + R)^{-\alpha} (1 + t + R)^{-\beta}, </math>

where

:<math> R = R(z, t) = \left(1 - 2zt + t^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}~,  </math>

and the [[principal branch|branch]] of square root is chosen so that <math>R(z, 0) = 1</math>.<ref name=sz/>{{Pg|location=IV.4}}

=== Other polynomials ===
The Jacobi polynomials reduce to other classical polynomials.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DLMF: §18.7 Interrelations and Limit Relations ‣ Classical Orthogonal Polynomials ‣ Chapter 18 Orthogonal Polynomials |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.7 |website=dlmf.nist.gov}}</ref>

[[Gegenbauer polynomials|Ultraspherical]]:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
C_n^{(\lambda)}(x) & =\frac{(2 \lambda)_n}{\left(\lambda+\frac{1}{2}\right)_n} P_n^{\left(\lambda-\frac{1}{2}, \lambda-\frac{1}{2}\right)}(x), \\
P_n^{(\alpha, \alpha)}(x) & =\frac{(\alpha+1)_n}{(2 \alpha+1)_n} C_n^{\left(\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right)}(x) .
\end{aligned}</math>[[Legendre polynomials|Legendre]]:<math display="block">P_n(x)=C_n^{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}(x)=P_n^{(0,0)}(x)</math>[[Chebyshev polynomials|Chebyshev]]:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
T_n(x)&=P_n^{\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)}(x) / P_n^{\left(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)}(1), \\
U_n(x)&=C_n^{(1)}(x)=(n+1) P_n^{\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)}(x) / P_n^{\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)}(1), \\
V_n(x)&=P_n^{\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)}(x) / P_n^{\left(-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)}(1), \\
W_n(x)&=(2 n+1) P_n^{\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)}(x) / P_n^{\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)}(1) . \\
T_n^*(x)&=T_n(2 x-1), \\
U_n^*(x)&=U_n(2 x-1) .
\end{aligned}</math>[[Laguerre polynomials|Laguerre]]:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\lim_{\beta \rightarrow \infty} P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(1-(2 x / \beta))&=L_n^{(\alpha)}(x) . \\
\lim_{\alpha \rightarrow \infty} P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}((2 x / \alpha)-1)&=(-1)^n L_n^{(\beta)}(x) .
\end{aligned}</math>Hermite:<math display="block">\lim _{\alpha \rightarrow \infty} \alpha^{-\frac{1}{2} n} P_n^{(\alpha, \alpha)}\left(\alpha^{-\frac{1}{2}} x\right)=\frac{H_n(x)}{2^n n!}</math>

=== Stochastic process ===
The Jacobi polynomials appear as the eigenfunctions of the [[Continuous-time Markov chain|Markov process]] on <math>[-1, +1]</math><math display="block">\mathcal{L}=\left(1-x^2\right) \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}+(p x+q) \frac{\partial}{\partial x} </math>defined up to the time it hits the boundary. For <math>p=-(\beta+\alpha+2), q=\beta-\alpha</math>, we have<math display="block">\mathcal{L} P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)} = -n(n+\alpha+\beta+1) P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}</math>Thus this process is named the '''Jacobi process'''.<ref>{{cite conference |last=Wong |first=E. |date=1964 |editor-last=Bellman |editor-first=R. |title=The construction of a class of stationary Markoff processes |url=https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wong/wong_pubs/wong10.pdf |location=Providence, RI |publisher=American Mathematical Society |pages=264–276 |book-title=Stochastic Processes in Mathematical Physics and Engineering}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Demni |first1=N. |last2=Zani |first2=M. |date=2009-02-01 |title=Large deviations for statistics of the Jacobi process |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304414908000458 |journal=Stochastic Processes and Their Applications |volume=119 |issue=2 |pages=518–533 |doi=10.1016/j.spa.2008.02.015 |issn=0304-4149|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Heat kernel ===
Let

* <math>J^{(\alpha, \beta)} := -\left(1-x^2\right) \frac{d^2}{d x^2}-[\beta-\alpha-(\alpha+\beta+2) x] \frac{d}{d x}</math>
* <math>T_t^{(\alpha, \beta)} := e^{-tJ^{(\alpha, \beta)}}</math>
* <math>h_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}=\int_{-1}^1\left[P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x)\right]^2(1-x)^\alpha(1+x)^\beta d x = \frac{2^{\alpha+\beta+1} \Gamma(n+\alpha+1) \Gamma(n+\beta+1)}{(2 n+\alpha+\beta+1) \Gamma(n+\alpha+\beta+1) \Gamma(n+1)}</math>
* <math>G_t^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x, y)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \exp (-t n(n+\alpha+\beta+1)) \frac{P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x) P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(y)}{h_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}}, \quad x, y \in[-1,1], \quad t>0,</math>
* <math>d \rho_{(\alpha, \beta)}(x)=(1-x)^\alpha(1+x)^\beta d x</math>

Then, for any <math>f \in L^1\left(d \rho_{(\alpha, \beta)}\right)</math>,<ref name=":3" /><math display="block">T_t^{(\alpha, \beta)} f(x)=\int_{-1}^1 G_t^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x, y) f(y) d \varrho_{(\alpha, \beta)}(y)</math>Thus, <math>G_t^{(\alpha, \beta)}</math> is called the '''Jacobi [[heat kernel]]'''.

=== Other properties ===
The [[discriminant]] is<ref>{{Cite web |title=DLMF: §18.16 Zeros ‣ Classical Orthogonal Polynomials ‣ Chapter 18 Orthogonal Polynomials |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.16 |website=dlmf.nist.gov}}</ref><math display="block">\operatorname{Disc}\left(P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}\right)=2^{-n(n-1)} \prod_{j=1}^n j^{j-2 n+2}(j+\alpha)^{j-1}(j+\beta)^{j-1}(n+j+\alpha+\beta)^{n-j}</math>'''Bailey’s formula''':<ref name=":3">{{cite arXiv | last1=Nowak | first1=Adam | last2=Sjögren | first2=Peter | title=Sharp estimates of the Jacobi heat kernel | date=2011 | class=math.CA | eprint=1111.3145 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bailey |first=W. N. |date=1938 |title=The Generating Function of Jacobi Polynomials |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/jlms/s1-13.1.8 |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=s1-13 |issue=1 |pages=8–12 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-13.1.8 |issn=1469-7750|url-access=subscription }}</ref><math display="block">\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(\cos \theta) P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(\cos \varphi)}{h_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}} r^n=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+2)}{2^{\alpha+\beta+1} \Gamma(\alpha+1) \Gamma(\beta+1)} \frac{1-r}{(1+r)^{\alpha+\beta+2}} \\
& \quad \times F_4\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta+2}{2}, \frac{\alpha+\beta+3}{2} ; \alpha+1, \beta+1 ;\left(\frac{2 \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \sin \frac{\varphi}{2}}{r^{1 / 2}+r^{-1 / 2}}\right)^2,\left(\frac{2 \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\varphi}{2}}{r^{1 / 2}+r^{-1 / 2}}\right)^2\right)
\end{aligned}</math>where <math>|r|<1, \alpha, \beta>-1</math>, and <math>F_4</math> is [[Appell series|Appel's hypergeometric function of two variables]]. This is an analog of the [[Mehler kernel]] for [[Hermite polynomials]], and the [[Laguerre polynomials#Hardy–Hille formula|Hardy–Hille formula]] for Laguerre polynomials.

'''Laplace-type integral representation''':<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dijksma |first1=A. |last2=Koornwinder |first2=T. H. |date=1971-01-01 |title=Spherical harmonics and the product of two Jacobi polynomials |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1385725871800264 |journal=Indagationes Mathematicae (Proceedings) |volume=74 |pages=191–196 |doi=10.1016/S1385-7258(71)80026-4 |issn=1385-7258|url-access=subscription }}</ref><math display="block">\begin{aligned}
P_n^{\left(\alpha, \beta\right)}\left(1-2 t^2\right)= & \frac{(-1)^n 2^{2 n}}{\pi(2 n)!} \frac{\Gamma(n+\alpha+1) \Gamma(n+\beta+1)}{\Gamma\left(\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\right) \Gamma\left(\beta+\frac{1}{2}\right)} . \\
& \int_{-1}^1 \int_{-1}^1\left(t u \pm i \sqrt{1-t^2} v\right)^{2 n}\left(1-u^2\right)^{\alpha-\frac{1}{2}}\left(1-v^2\right)^{\beta-\frac{1}{2}} d u d v .
\end{aligned}</math>

== Zeroes ==
If <math>\alpha, \beta > -1</math>, then <math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}</math> has <math>n</math> real roots. Thus in this section we assume <math>\alpha, \beta > -1</math> by default. This section is based on.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Harvard citation|Szegő|1975|loc=Section 6.21. Inequalities for the zeros of the classical polynomials}}</ref>

Define:

* <math>j_{\alpha, m}</math> are the positive zero of the [[Bessel function|Bessel function of the first kind]] <math>J_\alpha</math>, ordered such that <math>0 < j_{\alpha, 1} < j_{\alpha, 2} < \cdots</math>.
* <math>\theta_{n,m}=\theta_{n,m}^{(\alpha,\beta)}</math> are the zeroes of <math>P^{(\alpha,\beta)}_{n}\left(\cos\theta\right)</math>, ordered such that <math>0<\theta_{n,1}<\theta_{n,2}<\cdots<\theta_{n,n}<\pi</math>.
* <math>\rho=n+\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta+1) </math>
* <math>\phi_m=j_{\alpha, m} / \rho</math>

=== Inequalities ===
<math>\theta_{n, m}</math> is strictly monotonically increasing with <math>\alpha</math> and strictly monotonically decreasing with <math>\beta</math>.<ref name=":2" />

If <math>\alpha = \beta</math>, and <math>m < n/2</math>, then <math>\theta_{n, m}</math> is strictly monotonically increasing with <math>\alpha</math>.<ref name=":2" />

When <math>\alpha, \beta \in [-1/2, +1/2]</math>,<ref name=":2" />

* <math>
\theta_{n,m}^{(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{(m-\tfrac{1}{2})\pi}{n+\tfrac{1}{2}}\leq\theta_{n,m}^{(\alpha,\beta)}\leq\frac{m\pi}{n+\tfrac{1}{2}}=\theta_{n,m}^{(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2})}</math>
* <math>\theta_{n,m}^{(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2})}=\frac{(m-\tfrac{1}{2})\pi}{n}\leq\theta_{n,m}^{(\alpha,\alpha)}\leq\frac{m\pi}{n+1}=\theta_{n,m}^{(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}</math> for <math>m \leq n/2</math>
* <math>{\frac{\left(m+\tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta-1)\right)\pi}{\rho}<\theta_{n,m}<\frac{m\pi}{\rho}}</math> except when <math>\alpha^{2}=\beta^{2}=\tfrac{1}{4}</math>
* <math>\theta_{n,m}^{(\alpha, \alpha)}>\frac{\left(m+\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha-\tfrac{1}{4}\right){\pi}}{n+\alpha+\tfrac{1}{2}}</math> for <math>m \leq n/2</math>, except when <math>\alpha^2 = \tfrac 14</math>
* <math>\displaystyle\theta_{n,m} \displaystyle\leq\frac{j_{\alpha,m}}{\left(\rho^{2}+\tfrac{1}{12}\left(1-\alpha^{2}-3\beta^{2}\right)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}
</math>
* <math>\displaystyle\theta_{n,m} \displaystyle\geq\frac{j_{\alpha,m}}{\left(\rho^{2}+\tfrac{1}{4}-\tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2})-{\pi}^{-2}(1-4\alpha^{2})\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}
</math> for <math>m \leq n/2</math>

=== Asymptotics ===
Fix <math>\alpha > -1/2, \beta \geq -1-\alpha</math>. Fix <math>c \in (0, 1)</math>.

<math display="block">\theta_{n,m}=\phi_{m}+\left(\left(\alpha^{2}-\tfrac{1}{4}\right)\frac{1-\phi_{m}\cot\phi_{m}}{2\phi_{m}}-\tfrac{1}{4}(\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2})\tan\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\phi_{m}\right)\right)\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}+\phi_{m}^{2}O\left(\frac{1}{\rho^{3}}\right)</math>

uniformly for <math>m=1,2,\dots,\left\lfloor cn\right\rfloor</math>.

=== Electrostatics ===
The zeroes satisfy the '''[[Thomas Joannes Stieltjes|Stieltjes]] relations''':<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Marcellán |first1=F. |last2=Martínez-Finkelshtein |first2=A. |last3=Martínez-González |first3=P. |date=2007-10-15 |title=Electrostatic models for zeros of polynomials: Old, new, and some open problems |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S037704270600611X |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |series=Proceedings of The Conference in Honour of Dr. Nico Temme on the Occasion of his 65th birthday |volume=207 |issue=2 |pages=258–272 |doi=10.1016/j.cam.2006.10.020 |issn=0377-0427|hdl=10016/5921 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Harvard citation|Szegő|1975|loc=Section 6.7. Electrostatic interpretation of the zeros of the classical polynomials}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n, i \neq j} \frac{1}{x_{i} - x_{j}} &= \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\alpha+1}{1-x_i}-\frac{\beta+1}{1+x_i}\right)\\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n} \frac{1}{1 - x_{j}} &= \frac{n(n + \alpha + \beta + 1)}{2(\alpha + 1)} \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n} \frac{1}{1 + x_{j}} &= \frac{n(n + \alpha + \beta + 1)}{2(\beta + 1)} \\
\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n} x_j &= \frac{n (\beta - \alpha)}{2n + \alpha + \beta}
\end{aligned}</math>The first relation can be interpreted physically. Fix an electric particle at +1 with charge <math>\frac{1+\alpha}{2}</math>, and another particle at -1 with charge <math>\frac{1+\beta}{2}</math>. Then, place <math>n </math> electric particles with charge <math>+1 </math>. The first relation states that the zeroes of <math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}</math> are the equilibrium positions of the particles. This equilibrium is stable and unique.<ref name=":1" />

Other relations, such as <math>\sum_{1 \leq j \leq n, i \neq j} \frac{1}{(x_{i} - x_{j})^2}, \sum_{1 \leq j \leq n, i \neq j} \frac{1}{(x_{i} - x_{j})^3}</math>, are known in closed form.<ref name=":0" />

As the zeroes specify the polynomial up to scaling, this provides an alternative way to uniquely characterize the Jacobi polynomials.

The electrostatic interpretation allows many relations to be intuitively seen. For example:

* the symmetry relation between <math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}</math> and <math>P_n^{(\beta, \alpha)}</math>;
* the roots monotonically decrease when <math>\alpha</math> increases;

Since the Stieltjes relation also exists for the Hermite polynomials and the Laguerre polynomials, by taking an appropriate limit of <math>\alpha, \beta</math>, the limit relations are derived. For example, for the Hermite polynomials, the zeros satisfy<math display="block">-x_{i} + \sum_{1 \leq j \leq n, i \neq j} \frac{1}{x_{i}-x_{j}} = 0
</math>Thus, by taking <math>\alpha = \beta \to \infty</math> limit, all the electric particles are forced into an infinitesimal neighborhood of the origin, where the field strength is linear. Then after scaling up the line, we obtain the same electrostatic configuration for the zeroes of Hermite polynomials.

==Asymptotics==

=== Darboux formula ===
For <math>x</math> in the interior of <math>[-1,1]</math>, the asymptotics of <math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}</math> for large <math>n</math> is given by the [[Jean Gaston Darboux|Darboux]] formula<ref name="sz" />{{Pg|location=VIII.2}}

:<math>P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(\cos \theta) = n^{-\frac{1}{2}}k(\theta)\cos (N\theta + \gamma) + O \left (n^{-\frac{3}{2}} \right ),</math>

where

:<math>
\begin{align}
k(\theta) &= \pi^{-\frac{1}{2}} \sin^{-\alpha-\frac{1}{2}} \tfrac{\theta}{2} \cos^{-\beta-\frac{1}{2}} \tfrac{\theta}{2},\\
N         &= n + \tfrac{1}{2} (\alpha+\beta+1),\\
\gamma    &= - \tfrac{\pi}{2} \left (\alpha + \tfrac{1}{2} \right ), \\
 0 < \theta &< \pi
\end{align}
</math>

and the "<math>O</math>" term is uniform on the interval <math>[\varepsilon,\pi-\varepsilon]</math> for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>.

For higher orders, define:<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=DLMF: §18.15 Asymptotic Approximations ‣ Classical Orthogonal Polynomials ‣ Chapter 18 Orthogonal Polynomials |url=https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.15 |website=dlmf.nist.gov}}</ref>

* <math>\mathrm{B}</math> is the [[Beta function|Euler beta function]]
* <math>(\cdot)_m</math> is the [[falling factorial]].
* <math>f_{m}(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{m}\frac{C_{m,\ell}(\alpha,\beta)}{\ell!(m-\ell)!}\frac{\cos\theta_{n,m,\ell}}{\left(\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta\right)^{\ell}\left(\cos\frac{1}{2}\theta\right)^{m-\ell}}</math>
* <math>C_{m,\ell}(\alpha,\beta)={\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+\alpha\right)_{\ell}}{\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\alpha\right)_{\ell}}{\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+\beta\right)_{m-\ell}}{\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\beta\right)_{m-\ell}}</math>
* <math>\theta_{n,m,\ell}=\tfrac{1}{2}(2n+\alpha+\beta+m+1)\theta-\tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha+\ell+\tfrac{1}{2})\pi </math>

Fix real <math>\alpha, \beta</math>, fix <math>M = 1, 2, \dots</math>, fix <math>\delta \in (0, \pi/2)</math>. As <math>n \to \infty</math>,<math display="block">\left(\sin\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)^{\alpha+\frac{1}{2}}\left(\cos\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)^{\beta+\frac{1}{2}}P^{(\alpha,\beta)}_{n}\left(\cos\theta\right)
=
{\pi}^{-1}2^{2n+\alpha+\beta+1}\mathrm{B}\left(n+\alpha+1,n+\beta+1\right)\left(\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\frac{f_{m}(\theta)}{2^{m}{\left(2n+\alpha+\beta+2\right)_{m}}}+O\left(n^{-M}\right)\right)

</math>[[Uniform convergence|uniformly]] for all <math>\theta \in [\delta , \pi - \delta]</math>.

The <math>M = 1</math> case is the above Darboux formula.

=== Hilb's type formula ===
Define:<ref name=":2" />

* <math>J_\nu</math> is the [[Bessel function]]
* <math>
\rho=n+\tfrac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta+1)</math>
* <math>g(\theta)=\left(\tfrac{1}{4}-\alpha^{2}\right)\left(\cot\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)-\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)^{-1}\right)-\left(\tfrac{1}{4}-\beta^{2}\right)\tan\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\theta\right)
</math>

Fix real <math>\alpha, \beta</math>, fix <math>M = 0, 1, 2, \dots</math>. As <math>n \to \infty</math>, we have the '''Hilb's type formula''':<ref>{{Harvard citation|Szegő|1975|loc=8.21. Asymptotic formulas for Legendre and Jacobi polynomials}}</ref><math display="block">(\sin\tfrac{1}{2}\theta)^{\alpha+\frac{1}{2}}(\cos\tfrac{1}{2}\theta)^{\beta+\frac{1}{2}}P^{(\alpha,\beta)}_{n}\left(\cos\theta\right)=\frac{\Gamma\left(n+\alpha+1\right)}{2^{\frac{1}{2}}\rho^{\alpha}n!}
\left(\theta^{\frac{1}{2}}J_{\alpha}\left(\rho\theta\right)\sum_{m=0}^{M}\dfrac{A_{m}(\theta)}{\rho^{2m}}+\theta^{\frac{3}{2}}J_{\alpha+1}\left(\rho\theta\right)\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\dfrac{B_{m}(\theta)}{\rho^{2m+1}}+\varepsilon_{M}(\rho,\theta)\right)</math>where <math>A_m, B_m</math> are functions of <math>\theta</math>. The first few entries are:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
A_0(\theta) & =1 \\
\theta B_0(\theta) & =\frac{1}{4} g(\theta) \\
A_1(\theta) & =\frac{1}{8} g^{\prime}(\theta)-\frac{1+2 \alpha}{8} \frac{g(\theta)}{\theta}-\frac{1}{32}(g(\theta))^2
\end{aligned}</math>

For any fixed arbitrary constant <math>c > 0</math>, the error term satisfies<math display="block">\varepsilon_{M}(\rho,\theta)=\begin{cases}\theta O\left(\rho^{-2M-(3/2)}\right),&c\rho^{-1}\leq\theta\leq\pi-\delta,\\
\theta^{\alpha+(5/2)}O\left(\rho^{-2M+\alpha}\right),&0\leq\theta\leq c\rho^{-1},\end{cases}</math>

=== Mehler–Heine formula ===
The asymptotics of the Jacobi polynomials near the points <math>\pm 1</math> is given by the [[Mehler–Heine formula]]
:<math>
\begin{align}
\lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-\alpha}P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}\left(\cos \left ( \tfrac{z}{n} \right ) \right)    &= \left(\tfrac{z}{2}\right)^{-\alpha} J_\alpha(z)\\ 
\lim_{n \to \infty} n^{-\beta}P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}\left(\cos \left (\pi - \tfrac{z}{n} \right) \right) &= \left(\tfrac{z}{2}\right)^{-\beta} J_\beta(z)
\end{align}
</math>

where the limits are uniform for <math>z</math> in a bounded [[Domain (mathematical analysis)|domain]].

The asymptotics outside <math>[-1,1]</math> is less explicit.

==Applications==

===Wigner d-matrix===
The expression ({{EquationNote|1}}) allows the expression of the [[Wigner D-matrix#Wigner (small) d-matrix|Wigner d-matrix]] 
<math>d^j_{m',m}(\phi)</math> (for <math>0\leq \phi\leq 4\pi</math>)
in terms of Jacobi polynomials:<ref>{{cite book| last1=Biedenharn| first1=L.C.| last2=Louck| first2=J.D.|title=Angular Momentum in Quantum Physics|publisher=Addison-Wesley |location=Reading |year=1981}}</ref>

<math>d^j_{m'm}(\phi) =(-1)^{\frac{m-m'-|m-m'|}{2}}\left[ \frac{(j+M)!(j-M)!}{(j+N)!(j-N)!}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \left(\sin\tfrac{\phi}{2}\right)^{|m-m'|} \left(\cos\tfrac{\phi}{2}\right)^{|m+m'|} P_{j-M}^{(|m-m'|,|m+m'|)}(\cos \phi),</math>

where <math>M = \max(|m|,|m'|), N = \min(|m|,|m'|)</math>.
